newsitem.title: LATVIA: Pressure grows to recall Latvia PM to end crisis.
newsitem.headline: Pressure grows to recall Latvia PM to end crisis.

text.p: Several Latvian government parties on Wednesday called for Prime Minister Andris Shkele to stay in his job just two days after he quit amid a row with the Baltic state's president.
The calls came as controversial new Finance Minister Vassily Melnik, who sparked the row between Shkele and President Guntis Ulmanis which caused the premier to resign, himself quit.
The political crisis erupted after Ulmanis called on parliament to reject Melnik although he was backed by Shkele and the leading government party, the Democratic Party Saimnieks.
Shkele's resignation shocked Latvia, where many people saw him as important in speeding the reforms the small Baltic state has pursued since quitting the former Soviet Union in 1991.
The pressure on Ulmanis to keep Shkele grew as the president consulted political parties to find a new premier.
Saimnieks, the largest party in the country's eight-party coalition with 17 seats in the fractured 100-seat parliament, led the calls to reappoint the premier.
"Andris Shkele has to continue what he started, he has to continue reforms, he has to consolidate the nation," Samnieks leader Ziedonis Chevers told reporters.

Ulmanis had called on parliament to reject Melnik after reports that he had been investigated by the prosecutor's office under anti-corruption laws. The prosecutor's office confirmed the report but said it found no wrong doing.
Shkele resigned as he said the president and leading politicians had called his honesty into doubt.
Melnik told Reuters that he wanted to resign because of the trouble his appointment had caused. He also said he wanted to maintain government stability.
Two smaller government parties, the Farmers Union and the Christian Democrats Union, also said they wanted Shkele back.
Parliament's second largest party, Latvia's Way, had not yet decided but conceded Shkele's reappointment may be likely.

"The configuration of political powers makes Shkele's comeback highly probable although there are no guarantees given that the political consultations are not over yet," said Foreign Minister Valdis Birkavs, also Latvia's Way chairman.
Shkele, a non-party businessman, became prime minister at the end of 1995, a compromise candidate in a squabbling parliament that had already twice failed to form a government.
Shkele's coalition spans the politial spectrum but he managed to push through key laws despite internal bickering.
He has said his main aim was to solve Latvia's economic problems after a banking crisis in 1995 and has said his key achievement was passing a deficit-free budget in 1997.
Shkele has also pushed hard to speed the privatisation of key state companies and introduce other liberal economic measures.
